---

# Goal and Intended Audience

The goal of this project was to build an interactive dashboard where users can explore NBA team performance and payroll data from 2015 to 2024. Instead of just showing a fixed set of charts, I wanted users to be able to pick which teams they care about, choose which stats to compare, and filter by season so they can ask their own questions rather than just looking at whatever I decided to plot.

The main audience is basketball fans and anyone curious about how team spending relates to winning. I also tried to make it usable for someone who doesn't follow the NBA closely, so all the dropdowns use plain English labels like "Offensive Rating" instead of "ortg" and every chart has a caption showing where the data came from.

Honestly the reason I went with a dashboard instead of more static charts is that the data has 30 teams across 10 seasons and a lot of different variables, so there's no way a handful of fixed plots could cover everything interesting in it.

---

# Why I Chose This Approach

For Stage 3 I went with Option B and built a Shiny app. Shiny was on the suggested challenge list and I had never used it before since we didn't cover it in class. It seemed like the right fit because the whole point of my data is exploring relationships between different team stats, and an interactive tool is way better for that than a PDF with six charts in it.

Learning Shiny was harder than I expected at first. The biggest thing I had to get used to was that it doesn't just run top to bottom like a normal R script. You have to think about which parts of your code should re-run when the user changes something and which parts only need to run once. Once that clicked it got a lot easier, but it took me a while to wrap my head around it.

---

# Data

The dashboard uses the same cleaned dataset from Stage 2. It pulls from two sources:

- **Basketball Reference** (https://www.basketball-reference.com): team stats for all 30 NBA teams from 2014-15 through 2023-24, including wins, losses, offensive rating, defensive rating, pace, three-point attempt rate, and true shooting percentage.

- **HoopsHype** (https://hoopshype.com/salaries/teams/): total team payroll by season. The raw data is in dollars so I converted it to millions to make it more readable on plots.

After cleaning and merging everything in Stage 2, the final dataset has 300 rows, one per team per season, and 17 variables. I just load the cleaned CSV in the app so none of the data wrangling has to run again inside Shiny.

---

# Dashboard Features and Design Choices

The app has six tabs. All of them share a sidebar with a season range slider and a team selector, so you can set your filters once and they carry across every tab.

## Top Teams

This tab shows a ranked bar chart of teams by whatever stat the user picks. You can also control how many teams show up using a slider. Teams selected in the sidebar are highlighted in blue and the rest are grayed out.

I made it horizontal because team names are long and look really cramped on a vertical bar chart. I also added the actual values as labels on each bar so you don't have to squint at the axis. This tab came directly from peer review feedback, my reviewer said it would be useful to see top teams by name with financial info included.

## Compare Teams

This tab lets you pick specific teams and compare them either as a line chart over time or as a bar chart of their season averages. The line chart is better when you want to see trends, the bar chart is better for a quick side by side ranking.

I used the viridis turbo color palette here because it gives distinct colors even when a lot of teams are on the same chart, which gets messy fast if the colors are too similar.

## Scatter Explorer

This is probably the most useful tab. The user picks both axes so they can plot any two variables against each other. There's an optional regression line and an option to label the points with team names. I think being able to freely swap the axes makes this way more flexible than the fixed scatter plots in Stage 2.

When specific teams are highlighted their points get labeled. When nothing is selected I only label the most extreme outliers so the chart doesn't get too cluttered.

## Efficiency Dashboard

This tab shows four scatter plots in a 2x2 grid: offensive rating, defensive rating, true shooting percentage, and three-point attempt rate, all against winning percentage. I added this based on feedback from my peer reviewer who said the individual scatter plots should be grouped together. Having them all in one place makes it a lot easier to compare which metric has the strongest relationship with winning.

## Team Profile

This is my favorite tab. You pick one team and choose which stats to display and it generates a line chart for each one showing that team vs the league average over time. The league average shows up as a dashed gray line so you can immediately see if the team was above or below average each year.

This tab was the hardest to build because the number of plots changes based on what the user selects, so I had to figure out how to generate the layout dynamically inside the server instead of hard-coding it in the UI.

## League Trends

This tab tracks any stat across the whole league from 2015 to 2024. The solid line is the league average and the shaded band shows the range between the best and worst team each season. I added the shaded band because just showing the average hides a lot of interesting variation between teams.

---

# Methods and Technical Details

## Shiny Structure

A Shiny app has two parts: the UI and the server. The UI is just the layout, what the user sees and where the plots go. The server is where all the actual R code runs. I kept them clearly separated in app.R.

The main thing I had to learn was reactivity. I used `reactive()` to make a filtered version of the dataset that automatically updates when the season slider moves. Any plot that uses that filtered data re-renders on its own. I also used `observeEvent()` for the Select All and Clear buttons in the sidebar.

## Code Reuse

For the Efficiency Dashboard I wrote a helper function called `eff_scatter()` instead of copy-pasting the same ggplot code four times. It takes the variable name, title, and colors as arguments and returns the finished plot. Same idea as what we covered in the Programming lecture about writing functions to avoid repeating yourself.

I also wrote `var_label()` and `axis_formatter()` as small utility functions to handle label lookups and axis formatting in one place instead of scattering that logic throughout the server.

## Visualization Principles

I tried to apply what we learned in class throughout the app:

- Every plot has a title, subtitle, axis labels, and a data source caption.
- I used a custom theme function `theme_nba()` based on `theme_minimal()` so all the plots look consistent.
- Colors are used meaningfully, blue for highlighted teams and gray for background ones, with different color schemes for different tabs.
- I removed minor gridlines and redundant legends to keep things clean.

---

# Challenge: Learning Shiny

Shiny was my challenge for this project. I hadn't used it before and it isn't covered in any of the lectures. I mostly learned it by going through the official documentation at https://shiny.posit.co/r/getstarted/ and then just building the app one tab at a time and figuring things out as I went.

The hardest part was honestly just understanding why reactivity works the way it does. In a regular R script you just write code and it runs. In Shiny you have to wrap things in `reactive()`, `renderPlot()`, `observe()` etc. and it wasn't obvious to me at first why that was necessary. Once I understood that Shiny needs to track what depends on what so it knows what to re-run when an input changes, it made more sense.

The most annoying specific problem I ran into was the Team Profile tab. Because the number of plots depends on what the user selects, I couldn't just write a fixed layout in the UI. I had to use `renderUI()` to build it dynamically in the server. I also had to use `local()` inside a for loop which is something I'd never done before. Without it all the plots would end up showing the same variable because of how R handles scoping inside loops. That one took me a while to figure out.

---

# Conclusion

I think the dashboard ended up being a pretty useful tool for exploring the data. The six tabs cover most of the questions I'd want to ask about NBA team performance and the shared sidebar filters make it easy to focus on specific teams or seasons. If I were to keep working on it I'd want to add player level data and probably deploy it to shinyapps.io so you don't need R installed to use it.
